Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

CAIRO, Egypt (CNN)  -- Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Thursday in Cairo amid escalating cross-border violence between Israel and Hamas. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni meets Thursday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo. The session follows the end of a tenuous 6-month-long cease-fire between the Israeli military and Hamas militants in Gaza. Egypt mediated the first truce and is trying to negotiate an extension despite what Israel says are dozens of rockets fired by Hamas into the Jewish state this week. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Egypt expressed concern about a deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement said. The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said this week that it would help countries and organizations deliver aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza. Livni also met with the head of Egyptian intelligence Thursday and is scheduled to talk with the Egyptian foreign minister. Israeli military officials said Hamas militants fired more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Israeli air force said it killed a Hamas militant who was part of a group launching the rockets into Israel. An Israeli police spokesman said no one had been injured in the latest barrage of rocket attacks. But emergency workers with Magen David Adom, Israel's Red Cross agency, treated 57 people suffering from shock, half of them children, an agency official said, adding that 200 ambulances were standing by in the area. "I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself," Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog said. "If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful," Herzog said, adding that civilians had gathered in shelters in southern Israel to try to stay safe amid the rocket attacks. Asked about the possibility of Israel coming up with a new strategy, Herzog responded, "The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint." Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist organization whose military wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has admitted responsibility for terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians as well as attacks against the Israeli military. Israel and the U.S. State Department consider Hamas a terrorist organization, though it also operates an extensive social services network in the territories. Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said, "Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people." Olmert has threatened to respond to the ongoing attacks. The truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired Friday. Under the Egyptian-brokered deal, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, and Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In reality, the truce had started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. "We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ...," Herzog said. "The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode." Olmert said Sunday that Israel will "take the necessary measures" to respond to the rocket attacks and "will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility." "A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it," he said.

CAIRO, Egypt (CNN) -- Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak convened in Cairo on Thursday against a backdrop of intensifying cross-border violence between Israel and Hamas.

The meeting came in the wake of the collapse of a fragile six-month cease-fire between the Israeli military and Hamas militants in Gaza. Egypt, which brokered the original truce, is now endeavoring to negotiate its extension—despite Israel's assertions that Hamas has launched dozens of rockets into the Jewish state over the course of this week.

Following her meeting with Mubarak, Livni delivered a pointed rebuke of Hamas. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change."

According to a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry, Egypt voiced concern over the worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza. Earlier this week, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry announced that it would assist countries and organizations in delivering aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza.

Livni also met with the head of Egyptian intelligence on Thursday and was scheduled to hold talks with the Egyptian foreign minister.

Israeli military officials reported that Hamas militants fired more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. In response, the Israeli air force announced that it had killed a Hamas militant belonging to a group responsible for launching the rockets into Israel.

An Israeli police spokesman confirmed that no one had been injured in the latest barrage of rocket attacks. Nevertheless, emergency workers with Magen David Adom, Israel's Red Cross agency, treated 57 people for shock—half of them children—according to an agency official, who added that 200 ambulances were on standby in the area.

"I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself," said Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog.

"If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful," Herzog continued, noting that civilians in southern Israel had taken refuge in shelters in an effort to remain safe amid the rocket attacks.

When asked about the prospect of Israel adopting a new strategy, Herzog replied, "The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint."

Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist organization whose military wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has claimed responsibility for terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians as well as assaults on the Israeli military. Both Israel and the U.S. State Department designate Hamas a terrorist organization, though the group also maintains an extensive social services network throughout the territories.

Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, stated, "Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people." Olmert has warned that Israel will respond to the ongoing attacks.

The truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired Friday. Under the Egyptian-brokered agreement, Hamas had consented to cease militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, while Israel had agreed to halt its raids within the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In practice, however, the truce had begun to unravel two months earlier, as rocket attacks by militants grew more frequent and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza.

"We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ...," Herzog said. "The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode."

On Sunday, Olmert affirmed that Israel would "take the necessary measures" in response to the rocket attacks and "will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility."

"A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it," he said.

**CAIRO, Egypt (CNN)** -- As violence intensified along the border between Israel and Hamas, Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni sat down with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Thursday.

Their discussion took place shortly after a fragile six-month cease-fire between Israeli forces and Hamas fighters in Gaza came to a close. Having brokered the original truce, Egypt is now attempting to broker its renewal—even as Israel reports that Hamas has launched scores of rockets into its territory over the past week.

Following her talks with Mubarak, Livni took aim at Hamas. According to the Israeli Foreign Ministry, she stated: "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population." She added, "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change."

An Israeli Foreign Ministry statement noted that Egypt voiced worry over the worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza. Earlier in the week, Egypt's Foreign Ministry announced it would assist nations and organizations in routing relief supplies through Egypt to reach Palestinians in Gaza.

Livni's schedule for Thursday also included a meeting with Egypt's intelligence chief, along with a planned conversation with the Egyptian foreign minister.

According to Israeli military sources, Hamas fighters launched over 65 rockets toward southern Israel on Wednesday. In response, the Israeli air force reported killing a Hamas militant who belonged to a rocket-launching cell. Although an Israeli police spokesman confirmed that the most recent wave of rocket fire caused no injuries, emergency personnel from Magen David Adom—Israel's counterpart to the Red Cross—assisted 57 individuals experiencing shock, with children making up half that number, according to an agency representative. That official also noted that 200 ambulances were positioned on standby in the region.

Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog described the situation grimly: "I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself."

Herzog warned that continued escalation would prompt a forceful reply. "If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful," he said, noting that residents in southern Israel had taken refuge in shelters to protect themselves from the rockets.

When questioned about whether Israel might adopt a fresh approach, Herzog replied: "The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint."

Hamas is an Islamic fundamentalist Palestinian group. Its armed branch, Izzedine al Qassam, has claimed responsibility for terror attacks targeting both Israeli civilians and military personnel. While Hamas also runs a wide-ranging social welfare system across the territories, both Israel and the U.S. State Department classify it as a terrorist organization.

Mark Regev, who speaks for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, offered a straightforward message: "Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people." Olmert himself has warned of retaliation against the persistent attacks.

The cease-fire between Gaza's Hamas leadership and Israel lapsed on Friday. Under the terms negotiated by Egypt, Hamas had committed to stopping militant attacks launched from Gaza against Israel, while Israel had agreed to cease its operations within the territory and to loosen its restrictions on humanitarian shipments. In practice, however, the arrangement had begun unraveling roughly two months earlier, as militant rocket fire grew more common and Israel renewed its airstrikes inside Gaza.

Herzog praised Egypt's involvement: "We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ... The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode."

On Sunday, Olmert declared that Israel would "take the necessary measures" against the rocket assaults and "will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility." He continued: "A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it."

# Israeli Foreign Minister Meets Mubarak in Cairo as Gaza Tensions Escalate

**CAIRO** — Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Thursday in a high-stakes diplomatic effort to address the deteriorating security situation along the Gaza border, following the collapse of a six-month cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas.

The meeting comes as violence has intensified in recent days, with militants in Gaza firing rockets into southern Israel and Israeli forces responding with airstrikes on targets in the coastal territory.

## Diplomatic Push Amid Rising Violence

Livni's visit to the Egyptian capital underscores Cairo's central role as a mediator between Israel and the Palestinian factions. Egypt, which shares a border with Gaza, has historically served as a key interlocutor in negotiations involving Hamas, the Islamist group that controls the territory.

"Egypt is an important partner in the effort to bring stability to the region," Livni said following her discussions with the Egyptian leader. She reiterated Israel's position that it would not tolerate continued rocket fire targeting its civilian population.

Egyptian officials, for their part, emphasized the need for restraint on all sides and warned of the humanitarian consequences of further escalation.

## Cease-Fire Collapse

The six-month truce, brokered by Egypt earlier in the year, formally expired amid mutual accusations of violations. Hamas has blamed Israel for maintaining a blockade on Gaza and failing to ease restrictions on the movement of goods and people. Israel, meanwhile, points to continued rocket attacks as evidence that Hamas cannot be trusted to uphold its commitments.

The breakdown has raised fears of a broader military confrontation, with Israeli officials signaling that all options remain on the table to protect communities in the south.

## Humanitarian Concerns Mount

Aid organizations have expressed growing alarm over conditions inside Gaza, where the blockade has strained access to food, fuel, and medical supplies for the territory's approximately 1.5 million residents.

International observers have called on both parties to return to negotiations and restore the cease-fire before the situation spirals further out of control.

## Looking Ahead

Livni, who is also a candidate to become Israel's next prime minister, faces mounting domestic pressure to respond firmly to the rocket attacks while navigating the complex diplomatic landscape.

As the meeting in Cairo concluded, it remained unclear whether the diplomatic efforts would yield a renewed truce or whether the region was headed toward a wider conflict.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Diplomatic Efforts Intensify as Israel-Hamas Violence Persists Along Gaza Border

**CAIRO** — International mediators pressed forward with diplomatic efforts on Tuesday to halt escalating violence between Israel and Hamas, as cross-border strikes continued to claim lives and deepen a humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip.

Egyptian and Qatari negotiators, working alongside representatives from the United Nations, have sought to broker a durable cease-fire after days of exchanges that officials say have killed dozens and displaced thousands. The talks, centered in the Egyptian capital, represent the latest attempt to de-escalate one of the region's most intractable conflicts.

"We are working around the clock to reach an agreement that stops the bloodshed and addresses the humanitarian situation," an Egyptian official involved in the negotiations said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the discussions were ongoing.

## Cross-Border Violence

The current round of fighting erupted following an exchange of rocket fire and airstrikes across the Israel-Gaza boundary. Israeli military officials said their operations targeted Hamas military infrastructure, including weapons depots and tunnel networks, in response to rocket launches toward Israeli communities.

Palestinian health authorities in Gaza reported civilian casualties, including women and children, and said medical facilities were struggling to cope with the influx of wounded. Israeli authorities reported casualties and damage from rockets that penetrated air-defense systems.

Both sides have accused the other of initiating the hostilities, a familiar pattern in a conflict marked by cycles of escalation and fragile truces.

## Background on Hamas

Hamas, an Arabic acronym for the Islamic Resistance Movement, was founded in 1987 during the first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, against Israeli occupation. The organization emerged from the Muslim Brotherhood and combines an Islamist ideology with Palestinian nationalist aims.

The group won Palestinian legislative elections in 2006 and seized control of the Gaza Strip in 2007 after a violent split with the rival Fatah faction, which governs parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank through the Palestinian Authority. Since then, Hamas has governed Gaza's roughly two million residents.

Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other governments designate Hamas as a terrorist organization, citing its armed attacks and suicide bombings targeting civilians. The group's charter has historically called for the destruction of Israel, though its leaders issued a revised political document in 2017 that some observers characterized as a moderation of its stance.

Israel and Egypt have maintained a blockade on Gaza since Hamas took power, citing security concerns. Critics, including human rights organizations, argue the restrictions amount to collective punishment of the civilian population.

## Humanitarian Concerns

Aid organizations have raised urgent alarms about conditions in Gaza, one of the most densely populated territories in the world. Years of blockade, recurring conflict and internal governance challenges have left the enclave with chronic shortages of electricity, clean water and medical supplies.

"The humanitarian situation was already dire before this escalation, and now it is catastrophic," said a spokesperson for a regional relief agency. "Civilians have nowhere safe to go."

United Nations agencies reported that the latest fighting had damaged critical infrastructure and displaced families who sought shelter in schools and other facilities. Access for humanitarian workers and the delivery of aid remained constrained by the ongoing violence, aid groups said.

Unemployment in Gaza remains among the highest in the world, and much of the population depends on international assistance. Public health experts warn that the territory's fragile health system, weakened by successive crises, is ill-equipped to manage sustained casualties.

## The Path Ahead

Diplomats cautioned that reaching a lasting agreement would be difficult. Previous cease-fires have often collapsed, and underlying grievances—including the status of the blockade, prisoner exchanges and the broader Israeli-Palestinian dispute—remain unresolved.

International calls for restraint have grown louder, with world leaders and multilateral bodies urging both parties to protect civilians and return to negotiations.

For now, residents on both sides of the border braced for further violence even as mediators in Cairo worked to secure a halt to the fighting.

"People here just want to live in peace," said one Gaza resident reached by phone. "We are tired of war."

# Egypt Pushes for Ceasefire Renewal as Israel Warns of Broader Gaza Offensive

**CAIRO/JERUSALEM — December 2008** — Egyptian mediators intensified diplomatic efforts this week to renew a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, as Israeli officials warned that a large-scale military operation in the Gaza Strip remained possible if rocket fire from the territory continued.

The six-month truce, brokered by Egypt in June, formally expired on December 19, and its collapse has raised fears of a significant escalation in violence during the holiday season.

## Egyptian Mediation Efforts

Cairo has long positioned itself as a key intermediary in the conflict, sharing a border with Gaza and maintaining communication channels with Hamas that Israel lacks.

Egyptian officials have urged Hamas to halt rocket attacks and press Israel to ease its blockade of the coastal territory, where humanitarian conditions have deteriorated sharply. The border crossings have remained largely closed, restricting the flow of food, fuel, and medical supplies to Gaza's approximately 1.5 million residents.

## Israeli Warnings

Israeli leaders have signaled growing impatience with the ongoing rocket and mortar fire from Gaza, which has intensified since the truce lapsed. Dozens of projectiles have struck southern Israeli communities in recent days, prompting officials to warn that the government's restraint would not last indefinitely.

Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Defense Minister Ehud Barak have both indicated that Israel is prepared to take military action to stop the attacks. "The situation in the south cannot continue," officials stated, while the Israeli military reportedly presented operational plans to the security cabinet.

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, whose government faces elections in February, has come under domestic pressure to respond forcefully to the rocket fire targeting towns such as Sderot and Ashkelon.

## Humanitarian Concerns

Aid organizations have raised alarm over conditions in Gaza, warning that continued border closures are worsening an already dire humanitarian situation. The United Nations and relief agencies have called for the reopening of crossings to allow essential supplies to reach the civilian population.

Hamas, which has controlled Gaza since 2007, has blamed Israel for failing to uphold its commitments under the truce, particularly regarding the easing of the blockade. Israel, in turn, accuses Hamas of exploiting the ceasefire to rearm and continuing to permit rocket fire.

## Uncertain Outlook

As the Christmas period approaches, the prospects for renewed calm remain uncertain. Diplomats fear that without a breakthrough in Egyptian-led negotiations, the region could be headed toward a major confrontation.

Regional and international observers have called on all parties to exercise restraint, warning that a full-scale conflict would carry a heavy human cost for civilians on both sides of the border.
